en: Abhidhānottaratantra, Chapter 24 [Tibetan 27] = Lokesh Chandra facsimile edition [171.7] [1046']
Now I shall further explain the secret reality that is difficult to attain:
the origin of all mantras, the world of the moving and the stationary,
the supreme abode of all yoginīs, heroes, and Buddhas.

Inexhaustible, immutable, pure, and stainless from beginning, middle, and end; perfected as the wisdom of forms, the great bliss of Vajrasattva— three-faced, six-armed, peaceful, three-eyed, and the essence of compassion.
He is absorbed in the Mahāmudrā, pure and naturally stainless;
he sits with matted hair and a crescent moon, his head marked by a double-vajra (viśvavajra);
he wears a crown of skulls and is adorned by the five Buddhas.
Seated in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, adorned with the body-ornaments of the six mudrās, she is in union with the vajra and bell; her hands hold a sword and a hook,
while her divine hand holds a jewel-noose, bestowing all siddhis.
With faces white, blue, and red, the supreme abode of the three liberations,
the heart of the Jñānasattva, possessing the three wheels, he is the highest meditation;
the mind-wheel is indeed blue with the syllable HŪṂ, and his arms bear weapons.
The syllable KĀ is the wheel of speech, red, with its arms and weapons;
the syllable OṂ is the wheel of body, white, with its arms and weapons. United with the Vīras and Yoginīs, it is the stainlessness of body, speech, and mind.
One should contemplate Mahāmudrā at the center of the navel as the syllable *ikāra*.
With the syllable *īkāra*, one should visualize the lotus of the bhaga, which is as stainless as the moon of awakening (*bodhicandra*).
Having meditated on the syllable *ukāra* at the heart, one should place the syllable *ekāra* upon the head.
Having formed the armor with the syllable *aṃ*, [one places] the fierce son (*āmugraja*) with the syllable *aḥ*;
with the syllable *ṛṃ* is the goddess Locanā, and with the syllable *ṝ* is Samayatārā.
In the syllable *ḷ* is the goddess Paṇḍarā; in the syllable *ḹ* is Ratnasambhūtā, who holds a jewel-torch and is the lamp of gnosis.
She is white, with the color of a palāśa flower, and likewise red like refined gold.

They all have three faces, six arms, and three eyes; they are overwhelmed with passion, naked, and endowed with their own respective weapons. [The first holds] a wheel and a universal vajra, while the one born of jewels [holds] a jewel and a lotus.
She is joined with a bell, the bestower of all desires;
she holds a sword, an arrow, and a goad, and draws a supreme bow.
She is complete with all ornaments and is fierce with a skull-ornamented crown.
Seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), situated in the center of a universal lotus and moon, these [goddesses] are to be placed at the doors; in the center is the Lord upon a moon-seat.
In the corners, four goddesses are to be worshipped—naked, with disheveled hair.
She has three faces, six arms, and three eyes, and wears a garland of skulls;
she should hold a mirror in her right hand, while the other hands are as those of the presiding deity.
Complete with all ornaments, she is well-seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture;
her cheeks are touched by her palms joined in añjali, and likewise her hands are intent upon worship.
Thus, this all-knowing reality of the *āli*, which is utterly pure, secret, and extremely difficult to obtain, was spoken by Vajrasattva.
And the mantra-reality, according to the ritual rule, perfectly joined with body, speech, and mind:
Oṃ śrīmahāsukhavajrasattva āḥ a hūṃ ḍākinījālasamvara svāhā.
Oṃ siddhirocane! Ṛṃ a āḥ hūṃ svāhā!
Oṃ samāpattāre tutāre ture ṛ āḥ hūṃ svāhā.
Oṃ, O you born from the lotus, Pāṇḍaravāsinī! Ḷṃ ā hūṃ svāhā!
Oṃ ratnolkā ratnajālini ḷṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā.
Oṃ Rūpavajrī Bhrūṃ.
Oṃ Śabdavajrī hūṃ.
Oṃ Gandhavajrī Khaṃ.
Oṃ rasavajrī hrīṃ.
One should meditate upon the Omniscient Supreme Lord situated in the center of the *bhaga*,
the great secret *ālivajra* abiding in the hearts of all sentient beings.
One who reveals that which is secret and most secret among all phenomena,
and who is engaged in recitation and meditative cultivation as a yogi during the four junctions of the day;
The Great Being of firm vigor, free from all fear,
beholds the wheel of gnosis, which is the occasion for worship and consecration.
But through the state of a single flavor, by means of the yoga of emanation and reabsorption,
one [perceives] the entirety of the three realms as being like all the Vajra-holders.
"By means of those belonging to the future and the past within the three times— the present—
thus do the beings of the three times establish themselves in the state of Vajrasattva:
'The self, pure as co-emergent bliss, is supreme, without beginning or end.'"
The twenty-fourth chapter, on the Arising of Vajrasattva, in the Abhidhānottara.

[ 174.6 ] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a sentient being, a soul, or a person. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. He does not perceive forms, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, the nose-consciousness, the tongue-consciousness, the body-consciousness, or the mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. He does not perceive the earth element, nor does he perceive the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, or the consciousness element. He does not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death. He does not perceive suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of arhatship. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood, nor does he perceive the fruit of buddhahood. Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that he is called a ‘bodhisattva.’”
